{{short description|Concerns the decomposition of representations of a finite group into irreducible pieces}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Maschke's theorem''',<ref>{{cite journal |last=Maschke |first=Heinrich |date=1898-07-22 |title=Ueber den arithmetischen Charakter der Coefficienten der Substitutionen endlicher linearer Substitutionsgruppen |language=German |trans-title=On the arithmetical character of the coefficients of the substitutions of finite linear substitution groups |journal=<abbr Title="Mathematische Annalen">Math. Ann.</abbr> |volume=50 |issue=4 |pages=492–498 |url=http://resolver.sub.uni-goettingen.de/purl?GDZPPN002256975 |jfm=29.0114.03 | mr = 1511011 |doi=10.1007/BF01444297 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Maschke |first=Heinrich |date=1899-07-27 |title=Beweis des Satzes, dass diejenigen endlichen linearen Substitutionsgruppen, in welchen einige durchgehends verschwindende Coefficienten auftreten, intransitiv sind |language=German |trans-title=Proof of the theorem that those finite linear substitution groups, in which some everywhere vanishing coefficients appear, are intransitive |journal=<abbr Title="Mathematische Annalen">Math. Ann.</Abbr> |volume=52 |issue=2–3 |pages=363–368 |url=http://resolver.sub.uni-goettingen.de/purl?GDZPPN002257599 |jfm=30.0131.01 | mr = 1511061 |doi=10.1007/BF01476165 }}</ref> named after [[Heinrich Maschke]],<ref>{{MacTutor|id=Maschke|title=Heinrich Maschke}}</ref> is a theorem in [[group representation]] theory that concerns the decomposition of representations of a [[finite group]] into [[irreducible representation|irreducible]] pieces. Maschke's theorem allows one to make general conclusions about representations of a finite group ''G'' without actually computing them. It reduces the task of classifying all representations to a more manageable task of classifying [[irreducible representation]]s, since when the theorem applies, any representation is a [[direct sum of representations|direct sum]] of irreducible pieces (constituents). Moreover, it follows from the [[Jordan–Hölder theorem]] that, while the decomposition into a direct sum of irreducible subrepresentations may not be unique, the irreducible pieces have well-defined [[Multiplicity (mathematics)|multiplicities]]. In particular, a representation of a finite group over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] of [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] zero is determined up to [[isomorphism]] by its [[character theory|character]].

== Formulations ==

Maschke's theorem addresses the question: when is a general (finite-dimensional) representation built from irreducible [[subrepresentation]]s using the [[direct sum of representations|direct sum]] operation? This question (and its answer) are formulated differently for different perspectives on group representation theory.

=== Group-theoretic ===

Maschke's theorem is commonly formulated as a [[corollary]] to the following result:

{{math theorem
| math_statement = Let <math>V</math> be a representation of a finite group <math>G</math> over a field <math>\mathbb{F}</math> with [[Characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] not dividing the [[order (group theory)|order]] of <math>G</math>. If <math>V</math> has a subrepresentation <math>W</math>, then it has another subrepresentation <math>U</math> such that <math>V=W\oplus U</math>.{{sfn|Fulton|Harris|1991|loc=Proposition 1.5}}{{sfn|Serre|1977|loc=Theorem 1}}
}}

Then the corollary is

{{math theorem
| name = Corollary (Maschke's theorem)
| math_statement = Every representation of a finite group <math>G</math> over a field <math>\mathbb{F}</math> with characteristic not dividing the order of <math>G</math> is a direct sum of irreducible representations.{{sfn|Fulton|Harris|1991|loc=Corollary 1.6}}{{sfn|Serre|1977|loc=Theorem 2}}
}}

The [[vector space]] of complex-valued [[Class function (algebra)|class functions]] of a [[group (mathematics)|group]] <math>G</math> has a natural <math>G</math>-invariant [[inner product]] structure, described in the article [[Schur orthogonality relations]]. Maschke's theorem was originally [[mathematical proof|proved]] for the case of representations over <math>\Complex</math> by constructing <math>U</math> as the [[orthogonal complement]] of <math>W</math> under this inner product.

=== Module-theoretic ===
One of the approaches to representations of finite groups is through [[module theory]]. ''Representations'' of a group <math>G</math> are replaced by ''modules'' over its [[group ring|group algebra]]&nbsp;<math>K[G]</math> (to be precise, there is an [[isomorphism of categories]] between <math>K[G]\text{-Mod}</math> and <math>\operatorname{Rep}_{G}</math>, the [[category of representations]] of <math>G</math>).  Irreducible representations correspond to [[simple module]]s. In the module-theoretic language, Maschke's theorem asks: is an arbitrary module [[semisimple module|semisimple]]? In this context, the theorem can be reformulated as follows:

{{math theorem
| name = Maschke's Theorem
| math_statement = Let <math>G</math> be a finite group and <math>K</math> a field whose characteristic does not divide the order of <math>G</math>. Then <math>K[G]</math>, the group algebra of <math>G</math>, is [[semisimple algebra|semisimple]].<ref>It follows that every module over <math>K[G]</math> is a semisimple module.</ref><ref>The converse statement also holds: if the characteristic of the field divides the order of the group (the ''modular case''), then the group algebra is not semisimple.</ref>
}}

The importance of this result stems from the well developed theory of semisimple rings, in particular, their classification as given by the [[Wedderburn–Artin theorem]]. When <math>K</math> is the field of [[Complex number|complex numbers]], this shows that the algebra <math>K[G]</math> is a product of several copies of complex [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix algebras]], one for each irreducible representation.<ref>The number of the summands can be computed, and turns out to be equal to the number of the [[conjugacy class]]es of the group.</ref> If the field <math>K</math> has characteristic zero, but is not [[algebraically closed]], for example if <math>K</math> is the field of [[real number|real]] or [[rational number|rational]] numbers, then a somewhat more complicated statement holds: the group algebra <math>K[G]</math> is a product of matrix algebras over [[division ring]]s over <math>K</math>. The summands correspond to irreducible representations of <math>G</math> over <math>K</math>.<ref>One must be careful, since a representation may decompose differently over different fields: a representation may be irreducible over the real numbers but not over the complex numbers.</ref>

=== Category-theoretic ===

Reformulated in the language of [[Semi-simplicity|semi-simple categories]], Maschke's theorem states

{{math theorem
| name = Maschke's theorem
| math_statement = If {{var|G}} is a group and {{var|F}} is a field with characteristic not dividing the order of {{var|G}}, then the [[category of representations]] of {{var|G}} over {{var|F}} is semi-simple.
}}

== Proofs ==
=== Group-theoretic ===
Let ''U'' be a subspace of ''V'' complement of ''W''. Let <math>p_0 : V \to W</math> be the projection function, i.e., <math>p_0(w + u) = w</math> for any <math> u \in U, w \in W</math>. 

Define <math display="inline">p(x) = \frac{1}{\#G} \sum_{g \in G} g \cdot p_0 \cdot g^{-1} (x)</math>, where <math>g \cdot p_0 \cdot g^{-1}</math> is an abbreviation of <math>\rho_W{g} \cdot p_0 \cdot \rho_V{g^{-1}}</math>, with <math>\rho_W{g}, \rho_V{g^{-1}}</math> being the  representation of ''G'' on ''W and'' ''V''.  Then, <math>\ker p</math> is preserved by ''G'' under representation <math>\rho_V</math>: for any <math>w' \in \ker p, h \in G</math>, 
<math display="block">\begin{align}
p(hw') &= h \cdot h^{-1} \frac{1}{\#G} \sum_{g \in G} g \cdot p_0 \cdot g^{-1} (hw') \\
&= h \cdot \frac{1}{\#G} \sum_{g \in G} (h^{-1} \cdot g) \cdot p_0 \cdot (g^{-1} h) w' \\
&= h \cdot \frac{1}{\#G} \sum_{g \in G} g \cdot p_0 \cdot g^{-1} w' \\
&= h \cdot p(w') \\
&= 0
\end{align}</math>

so <math>w' \in \ker p</math> implies that <math>hw' \in \ker p </math>. So the restriction of <math>\rho_V</math> on <math>\ker p</math> is also a representation. 

By the definition of <math>p</math>, for any <math>w \in W</math>, <math>p(w) = w</math>, so <math>W \cap \ker\ p = \{0\}</math>, and for any <math>v \in V</math>, <math>p(p(v)) = p(v)</math>. Thus, <math>p(v-p(v)) = 0</math>, and <math>v - p(v) \in \ker p</math>. Therefore, <math>V = W \oplus \ker p</math>. 

=== Module-theoretic ===
Let ''V'' be a ''K''[''G'']-submodule. We will prove that ''V'' is a direct summand. Let ''π'' be any ''K''-linear projection of ''K''[''G''] onto ''V''. Consider the map 
<math display="block"> \begin{cases}
\varphi:K[G]\to V \\
\varphi:x \mapsto \frac{1}{\#G}\sum_{s \in G} s\cdot \pi(s^{-1} \cdot x)
\end{cases}</math>

Then ''φ'' is again a projection: it is clearly ''K''-linear, maps ''K''[''G''] to ''V'', and induces the identity on ''V'' (therefore, maps ''K''[''G''] onto ''V''). Moreover we have

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\varphi(t\cdot x) &= \frac{1}{\#G}\sum_{s \in G} s\cdot \pi(s^{-1}\cdot t\cdot x)\\
&= \frac{1}{\#G}\sum_{u \in G} t\cdot u\cdot \pi(u^{-1}\cdot x)\\
&= t\cdot\varphi(x),
\end{align}</math>

so ''φ'' is in fact ''K''[''G'']-linear. By the [[splitting lemma]], <math>K[G]=V \oplus \ker \varphi</math>. This proves that every submodule is a direct summand, that is, ''K''[''G''] is semisimple.

== Converse statement ==
The above proof depends on the fact that #''G'' is [[unit (ring theory)|invertible]] in ''K''. This might lead one to ask if the [[converse (logic)|converse]] of Maschke's theorem also holds: if the characteristic of ''K'' divides the order of ''G'', does it follow that ''K''[''G''] is not semisimple? The answer is ''yes''.{{sfn|Serre|1977|loc=Exercise 6.1}}

'''Proof.''' For <math display="inline">x = \sum\lambda_g g\in K[G]</math> define <math display="inline">\epsilon(x) = \sum\lambda_g</math>. Let <math>I=\ker\epsilon</math>. Then ''I'' is a ''K''[''G'']-submodule. We will prove that for every nontrivial submodule ''V'' of ''K''[''G''], <math>I \cap V \neq 0</math>. Let ''V'' be given, and let <math display="inline">v=\sum\mu_gg</math> be any nonzero element of ''V''. If <math>\epsilon(v)=0</math>, the claim is immediate. Otherwise, let <math display="inline">s = \sum 1 g</math>. Then <math>\epsilon(s) = \#G \cdot 1 = 0</math> so <math>s \in I</math> and 
<math display="block">sv = \left(\sum1g\right)\!\left(\sum\mu_gg\right) = \sum\epsilon(v)g = \epsilon(v)s</math> 

so that <math>sv</math> is a nonzero element of both ''I'' and ''V''. This proves ''V'' is not a direct complement of ''I'' for all ''V'', so ''K''[''G''] is not semisimple.

== Non-examples ==
The theorem can not apply to the case where ''G'' is infinite, or when the field ''K'' has characteristics dividing #''G''. For example, 

* Consider the infinite group <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> and the representation <math>\rho: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathrm{GL}_2(\Complex)</math> defined by <math>\rho(n) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^n = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & n \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}</math>. Let <math>W = \Complex \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1  \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}</math>, a 1-dimensional subspace of <math>\Complex^2</math> spanned by <math>\begin{bmatrix} 1  \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}</math>. Then the restriction of <math>\rho</math> on ''W'' is a [[trivial representation|trivial subrepresentation]] of <math>\mathbb{Z} </math>. However, there's no ''U'' such that both ''W, U'' are subrepresentations of <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> and <math>\Complex^2 = W \oplus U</math>: any such ''U'' needs to be 1-dimensional, but any 1-dimensional subspace preserved by <math>\rho</math> has to be spanned by an [[eigenvector]] for <math>\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}</math>, and the only eigenvector for that is <math>\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}</math>. 
* Consider a [[prime number|prime]] ''p'', and the group <math>\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}</math>, field <math>K = \mathbb{F}_p</math>, and the representation <math>\rho: \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} \to \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)</math> defined by <math>\rho(n) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & n \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}</math>. Simple calculations show that there is only one eigenvector for <math>\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}</math> here, so by the same argument, the 1-dimensional subrepresentation of <math>\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}</math> is unique, and <math>\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}</math> cannot be decomposed into the direct sum of two 1-dimensional subrepresentations.
